topics.title: Preoperative Localization
topics.frontClue: Guide the surgeon to a lesion they cannot feel: wire or wireless seed
topics.corePiece: Nonpalpable lesions or biopsy clips must be localized before surgical excision. With wire localization, a needle containing a hooked wire is placed under ultrasound or mammographic guidance, usually the day of surgery, so that the wire tip lies within or just beyond the lesion, ideally within about 1 cm, and the hook anchors it in place; the external end is taped and covered. Ultrasound guidance allows a shorter, more direct path that often parallels the chest wall. Wireless localization devices, such as radioactive iodine-125 seeds, magnetic seeds, radar reflectors, and radiofrequency identification tags, are implanted in the lesion and detected intraoperatively with a handheld probe; they can be placed days or more before surgery, improving scheduling and patient comfort. Bracketing with two devices marks the margins of larger lesions or calcifications. A post-localization mammogram documents the device position, and specimen radiography or ultrasound after excision confirms that the lesion, clip, and device were removed.
topics.whyLock: Localization is a team process, so communication and documentation dominate test items. The sonographer should report the distance from the device tip to the lesion and the skin entry site, because the surgeon plans the incision from them. Wire problems include migration, transection, and dislodgement before surgery, which is why wires are placed the same day and patients are told not to pull or bump them. A trap is assuming wireless seeds avoid radiation regulation; radioactive seeds require tracking and handling under radiation safety rules. Specimen imaging is the confirmation step.

topics.title: Procedure Complications
topics.frontClue: Hematoma is common; pneumothorax is rare and preventable with a parallel approach
topics.corePiece: Image-guided breast procedures are safe, but complications must be anticipated and managed. Hematoma and bleeding are the most common complications, more likely with vacuum-assisted devices and in patients on anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy; manual compression for several minutes after the procedure, typically about 5 to 10 minutes or longer, and ice packs reduce them. Infection is uncommon and minimized by aseptic technique. Vasovagal reaction, with pallor, sweating, nausea, bradycardia, and fainting, is managed by stopping the procedure, laying the patient flat, and raising the legs. Pneumothorax is rare and is prevented by keeping the needle parallel to the chest wall, especially in thin patients and with deep or axillary lesions. Other complications include implant rupture during biopsy near an implant, milk fistula when biopsying a lactating breast, pain, bruising, and very rarely needle tract seeding. Lidocaine allergy is rare, and patients should be asked about allergies before the procedure. Post-procedure instructions cover signs of bleeding and infection.
topics.whyLock: When a scenario describes a complication, match it to its cause and its fix. Expanding swelling after biopsy is hematoma: apply pressure. A patient who becomes pale and lightheaded is having a vasovagal reaction: lay flat and elevate legs. Shortness of breath or chest pain after a deep axillary biopsy suggests pneumothorax and needs urgent evaluation. A trap is attributing post-procedure fainting to lidocaine toxicity; vasovagal reaction is far more common. Displacing an implant away from the needle path, a technique similar to implant displacement mammography, reduces rupture risk.

topics.title: Informed Consent and Communication
topics.frontClue: Explain risks, benefits, alternatives; confirm patient and side; never give the diagnosis
topics.corePiece: Informed consent for an invasive procedure is obtained by the physician performing it and requires that the patient be competent, informed of the procedure's nature, its risks, benefits, and alternatives (including no procedure), and agree voluntarily. Consent is documented in writing, and a sonographer may serve as a witness. Before starting, a time-out following the Universal Protocol confirms the correct patient (two identifiers), procedure, side, and site, with the site marked when appropriate. Standard precautions, hand hygiene, sterile gloves, sterile gel, and sterile transducer covers are used for procedures, and transducers are cleaned and disinfected afterward according to manufacturer and facility protocol. Patient communication covers what to expect, how long it will take, comfort measures, and aftercare. Patient privacy is protected under HIPAA, and a chaperone may be offered. Sonographers describe the examination and its process but do not disclose diagnoses or interpretations; the interpreting physician communicates results. Anxious patients benefit from clear, calm explanations and the opportunity to ask questions.
topics.whyLock: Many patient-care items test scope of practice. If a patient asks whether the mass is cancer, the correct response explains that the radiologist will review the images and the results will come from the physician, without false reassurance or speculation. Consent cannot be obtained from a sedated or confused patient, and it may be withdrawn at any time. A trap is thinking the sonographer obtains consent; the sonographer may witness it. Another trap is skipping the time-out for a simple procedure; every invasive procedure needs one.
